title: Checkpoint: Shaping the Land
objective: After this level you can trace how water, ice, wind and gravity turn rock into the landscapes you see.
summary: One grain's trip from mountain to sea ties the chapter together: weathering frees it, ice or landslides move it, rivers carry it, and floodplains and deltas catch it.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: follow one grain from a mountaintop to the sea.
cards.body: Every level in this chapter was one leg of the same trip. Put them together and you can read almost any landscape.

cards.headline: Down the mountain
cards.body: High up, water freezes in a crack and wedges a chunk of granite loose. Carbonic acid turns its feldspar into clay, but the quartz survives. A glacier plucks the chunk away, or a rainstorm sends it down the slope in a landslide. Either way, gravity hands it to a river.

cards.headline: Down the river
cards.body: The river pushes the big grains along its bed and carries the silt in suspension. Where it slows, it drops them: sediment on the inside of bends, coarse grains on the levees, mud across the floodplain, and the rest at the mouth, where it builds a delta. Mississippi mud comes from a huge area: the river and its tributaries drain about 40% of the continental United States.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How water, ice, wind and gravity turn solid rock into the landscapes you see.
Why frost, roots and weak acid break rock apart, and why quartz survives as sand.
Where rivers carve valleys and where they drop their load to build floodplains and deltas.
Why hard rock stands as ridges, mesas and hoodoos while old mountains wear down.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land recap: about how much of the continental United States does the Mississippi River system drain?

options.label: About 10%
About 25%
About 40%
About 75%

questions.explanation: The Mississippi and its tributaries drain about 40% of the continental US, all or part of 31 states.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land recap: a granite chunk weathers for a very long time. Which of its minerals is most likely to reach the sea as sand?

options.label: Feldspar
options.rationale: Carbonic acid turns feldspar into clay.

options.label: Iron-bearing minerals
Quartz
Calcite
options.rationale: Calcite dissolves in weakly acidic water, as in caves.

questions.explanation: Quartz is very resistant to chemical weathering, so it survives the trip while feldspar turns to clay.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land recap: how does a glacier pluck rock from a mountainside?

options.label: The ice freezes onto bedrock and pulls pieces away
Meltwater dissolves the rock into the ice
options.rationale: Plucking is freezing and pulling, not dissolving.

options.label: Wind blows loose stones onto the glacier
The glacier melts the rock with pressure

questions.explanation: In plucking, ice freezes onto the bedrock and pulls pieces away as the glacier moves.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land recap: where does a flooding river drop its coarsest grains?

options.label: Far out across the floodplain
options.rationale: Only fine silt and clay reach that far.

options.label: Right beside the channel, building natural levees
Back upstream, against the current
options.rationale: Sediment is dropped downstream, where water slows.

options.label: Nowhere: floods carry everything to the sea
options.rationale: Floods drop sediment as they slow on the floodplain.

questions.explanation: Floodwater slows sharply as it spreads out, so the coarsest grains drop first beside the channel and build natural levees.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land recap: why do some rock layers stand up as ridges, mesas and hoodoos while others wear away?

options.label: Harder rock resists erosion better than softer rock
Soft rock is pushed up faster by plates
options.rationale: Plates don't sort rock by hardness.

options.label: Rain falls only on the soft layers
options.rationale: Rain falls on both; the rock responds differently.

options.label: Hard rock grows back after it erodes

questions.explanation: Differential erosion: resistant layers like caprock and tough sandstone wear away slowly and are left standing above softer rock.
